src.t: CNS Examination: Complete IMED Year 4 Notes

aka: Systemic inflammatory response syndrome with infection

faq.a: Yes, especially in the elderly, immunocompromised or with malaria; look for other systemic signs.
faq.q: Can sepsis be present with a normal temperature?

faq.a: Delays increase mortality; cultures taken first do not lose yield if antibiotics start promptly.
faq.q: Why give broad‑spectrum antibiotics before cultures?

faq.a: If MAP remains <65 mmHg after 30 mL/kg fluid bolus and lactate is rising.

exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer with HIV presents with fever, cough, RR 28, SBP 90 – what is the next immediate step? — Assess qSOFA, give 30 mL/kg crystalloid and start empiric ceftriaxone plus azithromycin.
How does septic shock differ from severe sepsis? — Shock requires vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg despite fluids.
What bedside sign helps differentiate sepsis from dengue shock? — Presence of a high‑grade fever with rigors favors bacterial sepsis; dengue often has a rash and severe thrombocytopenia.
Why is metronidazole added to ceftriaxone for intra‑abdominal sepsis in this setting? — To cover anaerobes common in perforated bowel, which ceftriaxone alone misses.
A patient’s lactate is 1.8 mmol/L but MAP is 60 mmHg after fluids – what does this indicate? — Persistent hypoperfusion despite a normal lactate; consider early vasopressors.
When should you stop antibiotics in a culture‑negative sepsis case? — After 48‑72 h if the patient is clinically stable, source is controlled, and no alternative source emerges.
What infection control measure reduces sepsis incidence in low‑resource hospitals? — Hand hygiene with alcohol‑based rubs before and after patient contact.
How would you manage sepsis in a patient with known severe renal impairment? — Use renal‑safe antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone), avoid nephrotoxins, monitor fluid balance closely.
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Sepsis is a life‑threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Early recognition, prompt antibiotics and supportive care are essential, especially where diagnostics are limited.

b: SOFA ≥2 indicates organ dysfunction
qSOFA ≥2 (altered mentation, RR ≥22, SBP ≤100) predicts high risk
sections.p: Sepsis is defined as suspected or proven infection plus a rise in the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score of ≥2 points.

b: Septic shock carries >40% mortality
Stage guides urgency of interventions
sections.p: Three tiers: Sepsis, Severe sepsis (organ dysfunction), Septic shock (requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg).

b: Gram‑negative bacilli from urinary/abdominal sources
Streptococcus pneumoniae for pneumonia
Plasmodium falciparum severe malaria can mimic sepsis
sections.p: In East African hospitals the common sources are: lower respiratory tract, urinary tract, intra‑abdominal infections, skin/soft‑tissue, malaria, HIV‑related opportunistic infections.

b: Rapidly progressive organ dysfunction
Look for source clues: cough, dysuria, abdominal pain
sections.p: Fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, altered mental status, hypotension, oliguria, warm flushed skin early, then cold clammy skin later.
Targeted tests to confirm infection, assess organ function and guide therapy.

t.b: Detect leukocytosis/leukopenia and anemia; high neutrophils suggest bacterial infection
Identify causative organism; if unavailable, treat empirically based on likely source
Elevated >2 mmol/L indicates tissue hypoperfusion; repeat to monitor response
Assess renal function; rising creatinine signals AKI
Detect urinary source; nitrites, leukocyte esterase, casts
Identify pneumonia, pleural effusion; if not available, rely on clinical signs

b: Persistent MAP <65 despite fluids
Bleeding diathesis, falling platelets
New oxygen requirement
sections.p: Uncontrolled shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute respiratory distress syndrome, acute kidney injury, secondary infections.

b: Give 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus within first hour; repeat if MAP still <65
Broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole for intra‑abdominal source)
If malaria suspected, give IV artesunate immediately
Consider antiretroviral therapy for HIV‑related sepsis after stabilization
Avoid nephrotoxic drugs (e.g., aminoglycosides) if renal dysfunction present
sections.p: Early bundle: fluids, antibiotics, source control, monitoring.

b: Educate patients on early care‑seeking for fever
Screen for HIV, TB, malaria in recurrent cases
sections.p: Monitor vitals, urine output, lactate, organ function daily. De‑escalate antibiotics based on cultures. Vaccinate against pneumococcus, meningococcus, influenza; improve infection control.

b: Malaria has periodic fevers and positive smear; treat with artesunate
Dengue shows thrombocytopenia and positive NS1 antigen
sections.p: Severe malaria, dengue shock syndrome, acute adrenal crisis.

b: Rely on clinical picture and repeat tests if suspicion remains
sections.p: Normal white cell count does not exclude sepsis; lactate may be normal early; malaria smear can be falsely negative if parasite load low.

whenToSeekHelp: Unresponsive patient, MAP <65 despite fluids, oliguria <0.5 mL/kg/h, rapidly falling platelets, new respiratory distress
